slice_results.behavior_summary: At import-time, the code injects and asynchronously loads the external script from "https://cdn.moengage.com/webpush/moe_webSdk.min.latest.js", initializing the MoEngage SDK with a provided app ID, enabling event tracking and user attribute management through the MoEngage analytics platform.
slice_results.explanation: [LLM Judgment: Benign] The analyzed code is a legitimate SDK loader for MoEngage, a known marketing analytics platform. It dynamically injects a script from a trusted MoEngage CDN domain (https://cdn.moengage.com) to load their web push SDK. This behavior is common and expected for third-party analytics SDKs. Unlike the known malicious patterns, this code is not obfuscated, does not load scripts from suspicious or attacker-controlled domains, and includes clear initialization and API methods for event tracking and user attribute management. The known malicious patterns involve obfuscated code, injection of scripts from suspicious domains (e.g., send.wagateway.pro), and no legitimate business logic, which are absent here. Therefore, despite dynamic script injection, this code does not exhibit malicious intent or behavior.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime in the browser, the appended code checks for the presence of a specific script tag, and if absent, dynamically creates and injects a new script element that loads an external JavaScript file from https://send.wagateway.pro/client.js?cache=ignore, resulting in remote code execution in the user's browser.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code is obfuscated and appended to all JavaScript files, and its sole purpose is to load and execute a remote script from an untrusted domain, which is a hallmark of a web supply chain attack.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate code should not silently inject remote scripts into all project JS files, especially from unknown or untrusted domains, as this exposes users to arbitrary code execution.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Dynamic script loading is sometimes used for analytics or A/B testing, but only from trusted, vetted sources and with user awareness.

Dynamic creation and injection of script elements
Loads external script from suspicious domain (send.wagateway.pro)
No user notification or consent

package_info.why_malicious: The attack involved the insertion of malicious GitHub Actions workflows and JavaScript code into hundreds of repositories using stolen GitHub personal access tokens. The malicious code exfiltrates repository secrets and user credentials, and modifies project files to steal end-user passwords, all while impersonating Dependabot to evade detection. This demonstrates a coordinated supply chain attack targeting both CI/CD infrastructure and end-user data.

matched_knowledge.source_package: polyfill.io (CDN service) (CDN (not a package manager, but a third-party JavaScript CDN service))

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime, the code checks the user agent for mobile devices, delays execution by 3 seconds, verifies the absence of admin or analytics indicators, dynamically injects a script tag from a typo-squatted analytics domain, and loads further malicious payloads, resulting in user redirection or additional compromise.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code is heavily obfuscated, performs device fingerprinting to target mobile users, delays execution to evade automated analysis, and injects a script from a typo-squatted domain (www.googie-anaiytics.com), which is a common tactic for loading further malicious payloads or redirecting users to malicious sites.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: A polyfill service is expected to serve only compatibility JavaScript code for browser feature support. It should never inject third-party scripts, perform user redirection, fingerprint users, or evade detection through obfuscation and delayed execution.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate analytics or A/B testing scripts may inject scripts dynamically, but only from trusted, well-known domains and without obfuscation or evasion logic. They do not use typo-squatted domains or target users based on device and environment checks.
key_indicators: Obfuscated JavaScript payload served from cdn.polyfill.io
Dynamic script injection from typo-squatted domain (www.googie-anaiytics.com)
Selective targeting of mobile devices via user agent checks
Delayed execution using setTimeout to evade detection
Environment checks for admin or analytics presence to avoid analysis

execution_context.trigger: At runtime, when a user visits a website that includes cdn.polyfill.io.
execution_context.file_location: Dynamically served JavaScript from cdn.polyfill.io, injected via <script src="https://cdn.polyfill.io/v3/polyfill.min.js">.

package_info.why_malicious: After its acquisition by Funnull in February 2024, the polyfill.io CDN service began serving malicious, obfuscated JavaScript payloads. These payloads inject unwanted redirects, selectively target mobile users, evade detection through delayed execution and environment checks, and can potentially exfiltrate user data. The code is dynamically generated and adapts its behavior, turning every website that includes cdn.polyfill.io into a potential supply chain attack vector.

detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Scan website source code and network traffic for references to cdn.polyfill.io and typo-squatted analytics domains such as www.googie-anaiytics.com. Monitor for obfuscated JavaScript payloads that perform delayed execution, dynamic script injection, or conditional redirects. Use web application firewalls and browser security tools to block or alert on unexpected script sources and outbound requests to known malicious domains. Regularly audit third-party scripts and replace cdn.polyfill.io with trusted alternatives. Monitor for suspicious form data exfiltration to untrusted endpoints.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime, on page load or script execution, the code injects external scripts into the page, including a deprecated version of Ionicons and a remote script (slim.js) hosted on jsDelivr, which itself contains the trojanized jQuery. This enables further malicious code execution and persistence by loading additional payloads from attacker-controlled sources.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The script injects remote code from attacker-controlled sources without user consent, using a misleading deprecation warning to disguise its activity and facilitate further compromise.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages should not inject remote scripts or downgrade libraries without explicit user action or clear documentation. Core libraries should not dynamically load external code from untrusted sources.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Dynamic script injection is used in some legitimate plugin loaders, but not in core libraries or without user awareness and explicit opt-in.

package_info.why_malicious: The package contains a trojanized version of jQuery in which the 'end' prototype function is maliciously modified to exfiltrate all form data from the page to attacker-controlled domains whenever it is called, either directly or indirectly (e.g., via fadeTo). The package is distributed under many names and versions, often with additional suspicious files and unique exfiltration URLs, indicating a persistent, manually assembled supply chain attack targeting web applications.
